360	We learn the laws of Pesach. It is not an obligation that every rabbi
361	in his community
362	must expound, 30 days before, and begin to teach them the laws of
363	Pesach. It is not necessary.
364	It is not an obligation. What people do is a custom.
365	But what the Gemara says, "they ask about the laws of Pesach,"
366	does not mean that every sage sits and studies the laws of Pesach, or
367	that every sage in the yeshivah, in the kollel, sits and studies the laws of
368	Pesach. Even those who learn in the kollel have a
369	fixed study schedule that they follow. They continue with their own study and are not
370	obligated to stop in order to study the laws of Pesach. Rather,
371	what is "they ask about the laws of Pesach"? Look, Maran did not
372	write "they expound,"
373	but rather "they ask about the laws of Pesach before Pesach."
374	What does "they ask" mean?
375	In the Tosefta, tractate Sanhedrin, it is written that when they
376	sat in the Beit HaVaad, as they called it, the place where
377	the sages gathered,
378	the Torah scholars would sit together and clarify
379	the halachot. One would get up and ask the Rosh HaSanhedrin: What is the law
380	in such and such a matter? He answers him, he must answer
381	him.
382	If there is someone who disagrees, he says to him, "You have
383	arguments, state your arguments." But generally,
384	when there is no disagreement, they continue, studying all
385	the halachot that they are asked, each one as it was asked.
386	But one must ask a thing in its time, not ask things
387	that are not related to the subject. If they are dealing with the laws of
388	Shabbat and one gets up and asks the laws of mourning, what does
389	mourning have to do with Shabbat? Why do you ask such questions? One does not
390	ask except about what they are engaged in.
391	One asks "ke'inyan" and is answered according to halachah: if a person asks on that same
392	subject, they answer him according to halachah. Otherwise it confuses
393	the rabbi, and instead of answering correctly, he answers
394	incorrectly, because his whole mind, his whole intellect was focused
395	on the matters they were dealing with, and suddenly he takes
396	him to another place, so an error can come from that. Therefore
397	one asks only at that hour, and he answers on the subject
398	as is proper. Therefore, if two people asked, one
399	asked a question on the subject
400	they were dealing with, the laws of Shabbat, and the second asked
401	not on the subject,
402	other questions, the laws of treifot, what do treifot have to do with
403	Shabbat,
404	and he heard both questions,
405	he is obligated to answer first the one who asked on the subject, and afterwards,
406	if he has time and wants to answer the second, who asked not
407	on the subject, he tells him afterwards, but first of all he must
408	give preference to the one who asked on the subject.
409	Now, when this is within the 30 days of Pesach, they were dealing with
410	the laws of Shabbat labors, but the rabbi, the rosh yeshivah, knows that this is
411	within the 30 days of Pesach and people are preparing for the festival of
412	Pesach and need to know the halachot. So he, by himself,
413	prepares and reviews all the laws of Pesach.
414	When they ask him, suddenly turning his attention from the laws of
415	Shabbat to the laws of Pesach, he answers them the laws of Pesach.
416	About this it is said "they ask about the laws of Pesach": the Pesach
417	of ours is the day,
418	you, the rosh yeshivah, the Rosh HaSanhedrin, should know that this is the time
419	when questions are asked, these are the laws of Pesach, and you must answer
420	them. Therefore it is not considered asking not on the subject. Go and place him
421	as one who asks on the subject.
422	This is how the Ran explains it. Therefore, what is written, "they ask about the laws of
423	Pesach," not "they expound": he says they are not obligated to
424	expound, but the rabbi alone is obligated to know everything
425	himself. It could be that he will be asked a practical halachah
426	about the wheat, they need to grind
427	it, about the baking they also need to know
428	the baking, to kasher the oven, to do the hagalah
429	of the utensils. All these things are laws of Pesach
430	that they ask him, and he answers. This is what it means, "they ask
431	about the laws of Pesach," all of this Pesach,
432	the 30 days, all these 30 days,
433	the matters of Pesach, as we said, a thing in its time. Therefore, when they hear
434	one who asks on the subject, this is the explanation.
435	The Mishnah Berurah
436	was not satisfied with it. Why did Maran omit the word "they expound"?
437	Why did he write only "they ask"? He says:
438	It is true that the Ran writes so, and Maran wrote like the Ran. What did
439	Rabbenu Nissim say? He said that it is literally written in the Gemara that on the subject
440	of the laws of Pesach, the matter is for the one who asks the sage.
441	That is what is meant by "ke'inyan": the whole thing is asking on the subject.
442	So he thought,
443	the author of the Mishnah Berurah, that the Ran is alone in this matter, and all
444	the sages do not hold this way. But this is not true, it is not correct.
445	The truth is like Maran. Therefore he wrote "they ask" and did not write
446	"those who expound" alone, the Ran.
447	So wrote the Rashba, he wrote like the Ran. Also the Ramban
448	wrote the same thing, that this is only about one who asks on the subject.
449	And so wrote also the Ritva.
450	The Ramban, the Rashba, the Ritva.
451	The Rashbatz, Rabbi Shimon ben Tzemach, also wrote the question
452	and the answer.
453	He wrote this
454	in his book Magen Avot. We have a book after the laws of Pesach as well, and there he also wrote
455	these things: one who asks on the subject only.
456	It is written "they ask the laws of Pesach," even more
457	than what we have. If you say that "they ask" means "they expound,"
458	that they must expound in public, there is a Gemara,
459	Megillah, that contradicts this. What is written there?
460	Our rabbis taught: Moshe established for Israel that they should expound
461	the laws of Pesach on Pesach, the laws of Atzeret on Atzeret, the laws of
462	each festival on that festival.
463	What does it say there? They taught that he established that they expound these laws. If
464	you say that 30 days before Pesach they ask, then
465	why the novelty of that same day? Surely there they expound. Rather,
466	surely it is not so; only on that day there is the enactment of Moshe
467	Rabbenu: Moshe spoke the festivals of HaShem to the children of Israel,
468	an enactment that we say all the laws of each festival, the laws of
469	Pesach on Pesach,
470	the festival of Shavuot on Shavuot. No, what are the laws of
471	Shavuot?
472	The laws there are, I mean, the laws of Yom Tov,
473	to tell them the laws of Yom Tov; there is nothing else there
474	to tell them. And the laws of each festival, the festival of Sukkot, those
475	laws of sukkah: which sukkah is kosher, which sukkah is invalid,
476	this is "the laws of each festival."
477	If so, if you say that 30 days before the festival they must
478	speak about the laws of the festival, then what is the novelty for us, Moshe Rabbenu?
